findings.summary: The page says moving a string invalidates pointers and iterators, and explains it only by inline bytes. That is true for SSO strings but not for heap strings.
findings.evidence: "Invalidated by move, swap, growth" and "Why do iterators die on move? Inline bytes move with the object"
findings.fix: Say that moving an SSO string invalidates pointers and iterators because the bytes are copied to the new object. For heap strings, move construction normally leaves them valid, now pointing into the new owner. Swap and growth are the other common invalidators.

findings.summary: The move row says std::move copies inline bytes, yet the Q&A answers that iterators die on move because 'Inline bytes move with the object', which is terse and unclear for the heap case.
findings.evidence: Why do iterators die on move? Inline bytes move with the object
findings.fix: Answer for both cases: 'SSO: bytes copied to a new object; heap: pointer stolen, so old iterators point at a moved-from string'.
